title: Walt Disney (DIS) Q4 2026 Earnings Call Transcript
transcript:
Streaming profits surged, but Asian park attendance remained a clear drag.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Nov. 17, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

TAKEAWAYS

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email[email protected]

RISKS

SUMMARY

The Walt Disney Company(DIS-0.79%)reported fiscal 2026 results that met or exceeded guidance across primary financial metrics. Management reported that growth was driven by continued momentum in the streaming business and record attendance at domestic theme parks. The company indicated a strategic focus on three priorities: storytelling, technological innovation, and operating as a unified enterprise. Management reported that investments in fiscal 2027 will prioritize international content, the expansion of the Disney Cruise Line fleet, and the integration of advanced technologies to improve guest experiences and operational efficiency.

Full Conference Call Transcript

These forward-looking statements, including regarding the company's future business plans, prospects and financial performance are not historical in nature and are based on management's assumptions regarding the future and are subject to risks and uncertainties, including, among other factors: economic, geopolitical, operating and industry conditions, legal and regulatory developments and the company's decisions. Refer to our IR website.

The earnings release and the risks and uncertainties described in our 10-K issued today and subsequent filings with the SEC for more information on the risks that could cause results to differ. A reconciliation of certain non-GAAP measures referred to on this webcast to the most comparable GAAP measures is on our IR website.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Good morning, and welcome to The Walt Disney Company's Fiscal Fourth Quarter and Full Year 2026 Earnings Call. Thank you for joining us. I'm Ben Swinburne, Executive Vice President of Investor Relations and Corporate Strategy. With me today are Josh D'Amaro, our Chief Executive Officer; and Hugh Johnston, our Chief Financial Officer. We will begin today's call with prepared remarks from Josh. After Josh's remarks, we will take your questions. With that, let me turn the call over to Josh.

Josh D’Amaro:Thanks, Ben, and good morning, everyone. Fiscal 2026 was a defining year for The Walt Disney Company. At a moment of real change, we stayed focused on delivering for our fans, creating value for our shareholders and building on the momentum of this extraordinary company. That focus is visible in the results that we released this morning, and I am proud of how this entire team has executed against our strategy. Disney isn't just the world's leading entertainment company, we're a growth company. Our fiscal 2026 results back that up. We delivered them in a pivotal year for Disney and in a challenging macroeconomic environment.

We closed this year with a strong fourth quarter, exceeding our Q4 total segment OI guidance. But the broader picture is best understood by looking at the full year and across the enterprise rather than any single quarter or segment. For fiscal 2026, we're pleased to have delivered 7% revenue growth, 10% total segment OI growth and 16% adjusted EPS growth, all excluding the impact of the 53rd week. This success reflects our continued execution across 3 strategic priorities: World-class storytelling as our North Star; technology in service of our storytellers and our fans; and operating as One Disney. That third priority is also how we run our company.

It brings our businesses together around fandom and makes the first 2 priorities worth more together than apart. Disney is built for the modern entertainment industry. We have a healthy balance sheet, a clear growth trajectory in streaming, a growing experience business, a leadership position in sports, and iconic brands with deep consumer relationships across both the physical and digital worlds. And as consumer behavior shifts, traditional businesses face pressure and the fight for growth intensifies, our edge is how these businesses connect. For proof of this, you don't have to look any further than Marvel and the enduring power of the Avengers franchise.

We are so excited about Avengers: Doomsday, which arrives in theaters December 18, and we're pleased with the early presales. Following the drop of the Doomsday trailer this summer, along with the global theatrical success of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, August was the highest month ever for Marvel Studios viewing on Disney+. And during the quarter, Marvel viewership on Disney+ more than doubled compared to its historic baseline. That momentum reflects how One Disney turns a great story into more opportunities for fans to engage. Marvel Cinematic Universe films have now generated more than $35 billion at the global box office. Following its rerelease in late September, Avengers: Endgame is once again the highest grossing film of all time.

And a hit like this doesn't stop at the box office, it extends across streaming, consumer products, games, social and at our parks, hotels and on our cruise ships. Beyond Marvel, this year, we've taken action on every front to set up the next phase of growth. We brought marketing and brand together under one leader for the first time. We named a single leader for Disney+. We moved consumer products into Entertainment so that our stories and our products work as one. We hired our first Chief Technology Officer. We brought more sports to Disney+ and expanded our college football rights. We committed to more international content.

We signed a first-of-its-kind agreement with TikTok to bring creators into our stories. And we kept building at our parks and announced what's coming next. Now let me show you how that's playing out across the entire company. As we enter fiscal 2027, we continue to deliver on our financial commitments. In 2024, we gave 3-year adjusted EPS growth guidance. Two years in, we're ahead of that schedule. And today, we're reiterating our expectations for double-digit adjusted EPS growth in fiscal 2027, excluding the impact of the 53rd week. This track record reflects how execution focused we are as a company, and we intend to keep it that way.

Now to the core growth drivers behind these results starting with streaming. We are pleased with our progress this quarter. We saw healthy growth in engagement on Disney+ with notable strength across EMEA, Lat Am and APAC, increasing the time our fans spend on these services will benefit retention and ultimately, revenue growth. All of this starts with great content and our creative teams delivered across film and television. In film, Toy Story 5 crossed the $1 billion mark at the global box office. And The Devil Wears Prada 2, it earned close to $700 million worldwide.

In television, Furious emerged as a breakout scripted hit and Dancing with the Stars had its strongest start in 6 years, up 24% over the prior season. Scaling Disney+ outside of the U.S., it's a major opportunity. Our local originals are already making an impact. Our latest breakout hit from South Korea, The Remarried Empress, which debuted November 3. It was the biggest premiere ever for a local original across Disney+ and Hulu globally. And we haven't even begun to see the benefits of our plans to invest more in international content. Investments will deepen engagement over time, increasing lifetime fan value.

The power of live sports can be seen in ESPN's strong quarter, highlighted by 20% advertising growth with a 53rd week contributing approximately 5%. We're thrilled to welcome back both college football and the NFL with continued rating strength across both. Monday Night Football ratings in the quarter were up 20% over the prior year, and we broadcast the highest rated U.S. Open tennis since 2022. In February, ESPN will host its first-ever Super Bowl as we harness the promotional power and reach of Disney's many businesses to build excitement and deepen fandom for football globally, with the Super Bowl available on ESPN, ABC, ESPN Deportes, the ESPN App and on Disney+.

And earlier this month, we expanded our College Football Playoff rights, starting in 2027, the playoffs grow from 11 games to 23, and ESPN remains its exclusive rights holder with more games on ABC. Live sports remain among the most powerful ways to bring fans together, and ESPN is the place of record for sports fans. At Disney Experiences, we again delivered in the quarter with strong growth in global guests of 4%, excluding the 53rd week, and we did that despite increasing macroeconomic headwinds impacting our Shanghai and Hong Kong parks. In fact, fiscal '26 set a new all-time record for global guests at Disney Experiences.

In our domestic Parks & Experiences, strong revenue growth was driven by both rate and volume, reflecting the value that we provide to our guests and the benefits of our capacity expansion program. These results underscore how differentiated a Disney Vacation is for our fans and reinforces our confidence in the attractive returns we can generate from our investments. We're also investing with discipline to drive further growth in the years ahead, and we're concentrating that investment in our 2 biggest growth areas, streaming and Experiences. In streaming, we intend to bring more of our world-class entertainment and sports content to a growing fan base around the world.

We plan to increase content spending in fiscal 2027 compared to fiscal 2026, driven in part by the increase in international local content for Disney+ that I mentioned earlier. In Experiences, the capital plan we announced in 2023 is well underway with new projects being built across our portfolio. That plan will continue to expand our capacity and deliver a differentiated entertainment experience as we continue turbocharging our parks and cruise businesses. Of course, technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment. Our product teams have made meaningful improvements to the Disney+ user experience, and we're seeing the impact in our financial results.

ESPN remains an innovation hub for the entire company. Verts on ESPN set back-to-back monthly records in September and October. And these are just a few of the examples of how product innovation can deepen engagement across Disney. As I mentioned earlier, we hired our first Chief Technology Officer, Karan Anand. Karan is a lifelong Disney fan. And in his first weeks, he's been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better. working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses, always in service of our storytellers. We are thrilled to have him on board.

Last quarter, we talked about the work underway to make us more efficient. As we said in today's letter, we now expect that work to deliver approximately $3 billion in annual run rate savings by fiscal 2029. Most of those savings will be used to fund future growth. Now changes like these are not easy, and they affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company. At the same time, these steps are important if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth.

We make these choices because we believe so strongly in what Disney can be. So let me close with why I'm so confident. No company in entertainment has what we have, a library of stories and characters that grows every year and stays with fans for life. Marvel, Pixar, Star Wars, Disney Animation and the franchises that we're building next. A set of businesses that meet fans wherever they are, whether in a theater or on a screen, at a game or in a game, in a park or on a ship and a commitment to innovation and excellence that shows up in everything we make and every guest we serve. Each of those is a strength on its own.

Together, they compound. A great story becomes a film, a series, a ride, a product, a moment fans share, and each one gives a fan another reason to come back. That is One Disney. It's why we're so well positioned to lead for decades to come. I'm more optimistic about Disney's future than I have ever been. We have the stories, the reach and the discipline to keep earning the trust of our fans. Finally, I'm pleased to announce that we'll host an investor event in May 2027, where we'll provide a deeper look at our long-term strategy and further define our growth opportunity. Of course, we look forward to seeing many of you there.

With that, let me turn the call back to Ben for analyst Q&A.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Thanks, Josh. Before we turn to Q&A, I want to mention that as highlighted in our shareholder letter and beginning with the first fiscal quarter of 2027, we'll update our disclosure to reflect the shift of consumer products, excluding branded retail, from Disney Experiences to Disney Entertainment, to provide additional revenue disclosure at Disney Entertainment and to exclude equity income from our Entertainment segment operating results. We are providing supplemental financial information reflecting these changes available on our Investor Relations website.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:All right. We're going to begin our Q&A with questions on our Experiences segment. First question comes from Ric Prentiss of Raymond James. Ric asks, several big additions coming to the Orlando and other parks in the near to midterm, which ones are the most significant in terms of new capacity? And do you see those as growth accelerators or primarily to maintain current growth levels? Any thoughts or insights on the return of capital targets? Josh, do you want to take that one?

Josh D’Amaro:Yes, I'll take that. Thanks for the question, Ric. Maybe before I answer the question, I understand from my team that you are retiring soon, and that you've done something like 120 earnings calls. I don't know what to say about that, but congratulations to you. We obviously wish you all the best. Back to your question. So before I answer it directly, maybe I'll just take a beat here and reflect on the year that we just had. It was a great one. We had a new record number of guests come to our attractions all around the world. And yes, you're right, there's a lot going on right now.

We have more projects underway all around the world at any other point in the history of the segment. And a lot of that is actually focused right at -- in Orlando at Walt Disney World. I was just there recently, and I get a chance to go every once in a while and walk the projects under construction. And I got to say the Imagineers are just -- they're doing an incredible job over delivering on creative expectations that I have and the scale and the detail across all the expansion that's taking place there. It's really incredible. The last stop on my trip was at Monstropolis, which is at the studio. And it's again, the scale is fantastic.

It's just stunning. I think once we get a chance to open this up to guests, they're going to love it. We shared this in the past, these additions, all this expansion, it comes online over a period of time. The first phase of it with things like Monstropolis that I just mentioned, Lakeshore Lodge and Tropical Americas, which is Animal Kingdom, they all open in calendar 2027. And we haven't announced the dates on some of the other things like new Cars -- the new Cars Land and Villains Land at Magic Kingdom but they will follow after that.

If we go to the West Coast in Anaheim, Avengers Campus, which is at Disney California Adventure, that's going to double in size by 2028. So a pretty significant expansion there. And as this group knows, we're investing across all of our international parks as well. Now each of these are expected to contribute to growth. Some of the projects will add capacity to the parks that they're in. Others will give guests more reason to come and visit, maybe they'll stay longer. Hopefully, they spend a little bit more or do some of all of those things. And of course, that's going to let us grow both volume and yield, which you've seen in our results.

And then on returns, we stay disciplined. Every project is going to go through a rigorous review. Each one has clear return expectations. We're not adding capacity for its own sake, we pair that with strong guest demand. And as I had mentioned last quarter, we're investing to deliver double-digit returns over the lifetime of these projects.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. Next question is from Jessica Reif Ehrlich from BofA. Jessica asks, Experience is in the middle of one of the largest expansions ever. Cruise state room capacity is up roughly 50% with Destiny and Adventure. Fleet is heading towards 13 ships over the next 5 years, and you're adding new attractions at Walt Disney World in 2027. So the question is, how confident are you that demand keeps pace without leaning on promotions? Specifically, what are advanced bookings telling you about yield on the new ships, especially in Asia, where your parks are soft? How do you sustain segment margins through a period of heavy preopening costs and new capacity?

Josh D’Amaro:That's for me.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:That's for you, Josh. Yes, sorry.

Josh D’Amaro:Okay. All right. Well, thanks, Jessica. All right. So you asked about demand keeping pace with the added capacity. First, remember, we are a small -- really small share of the global cruise industry today. And we've got really unique competitive advantages in this market. Our cruise line, it draws on all the great IP that we have and the connection that we have with our fans and our guests. So we think that there's a lot of room to grow on this front. The real limit, I guess, on how fast we grow cruise is it's shipbuilding capacity itself, not necessarily the market opportunity. Hugh and I talk about this a lot.

We would add more ships if we could get ones that meet the standards that we have. And then this business, cruise, it's really flexible. We can add, we can reposition capacity faster than we can build land-based resort and that lets us reach new guests and go to new markets. By the way, just as an example, next summer, the Disney Wish sails in the U.K. and Europe. So we've got a lot of flexibility on that front. On your question about Asia, so we called out consumer pressure at our Shanghai and Hong Kong parks in the letter. And we're expecting that will continue into fiscal '27.

I think it's worth mentioning in the fourth quarter, strength at our domestic parks and at Disneyland Paris, it more than offset that weakness. And this is just a byproduct of our portfolio, which really is built to absorb these kinds of swings in specific market conditions. Now we're entering our second year with the Adventure. So it's too early to tell if the macro weakness is impacting demand for that single ship. But for the rest of the fleet, when we look at booked occupancy, it's actually holding up pretty nicely even with the additional capacity that we brought online. So we feel good about forward cruise bookings. And then margins.

So lastly, on the margin side, we don't break out cruise specifically, but what we have done is grown our margins in our domestic Parks & Experiences by just about 300 basis points over the last 10 years. And we have to, of course, think about preopening costs as a normal part of launching new ships and attractions. So I think I covered most of them.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Yes. Okay. Hugh, this is for you from Laura Martin at Needham. With Disney several years into its $60 billion 10-year capital investment program, can you talk us through the relative ROIC of parks versus cruise ships, and whether we eventually reach a saturation point where there is cannibalization between the 2?

Hugh Johnston:Yes. Great. Thanks for the question, Laura. A lot of questions on cruises and parks this morning. We believe we're uniquely positioned because of the breadth and connectivity of the portfolio that we have. And in a lot of ways, cruise is a great example of that. On the one hand, we have a large funnel of fans that enjoy the land-based offerings and then we can introduce them into the Cruise Lines. At the same time, by virtue of the mobility of the Cruise Lines, it allows us to reach new geographies and new guests that might not otherwise be able to get to our parks.

And that kind of reinforces why we see parks and cruises as complementary growth platforms rather than competing investments. As Josh mentioned earlier, we're really turbocharging the business at a faster pace than we have historically. And the ROIC is a mix of the mature cash-generating investments along with projects that are still work in process or under development. If you look only at the assets that are open and operating, returns remain really strong, and we expect that strength to carry through as the new investments come online as well.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. Thank you, Hugh. I guess as a retirement gift, we've got another question from Ric. I think, Josh, for you. As everyone is aware, there's been a divergence recently in Disney's domestic parks performance versus the competition. What can we attribute that to? And how sustainable is that trend?

Josh D’Amaro:Okay. Again, thanks, Ric. Actually, I'm glad you noticed that. I mean, listen, for more than 70 years now, our parks have been how families spend time together. And that connection that we have with our fans, it's just a huge reason that we stand apart from anyone else. Of course, we bring the best IP in the world and that IP just keeps that flywheel spinning and giving people and fans, new reasons to engage with us. And yes, I mean, the business is good. We saw healthy growth in both volume and per capita spending at Walt Disney World this summer. And if you look at domestic parks in the quarter, volume was up.

So attendance was up 3%. That's excluding the 53rd week and per caps were also up, they were up 4%. And when you step back and look at it, there are a few things that are driving this growth. First, I think it's so clear, fans just value the Disney Experiences, and there really isn't anything out there that matches it. And in many ways, Experiences is where our flywheel and our super fans, they come together most clearly, and you see it in our financial results. Second, consumers want real Experiences now. And I think that we're seeing that accelerate. People today are spending so much of their lives on screens.

They're just looking for time to connect with each other in the real world. And I think Disney is -- a Disney park, it's one of the few places that you can actually do that. We deliver on that at scale, and that puts us in a very different position from almost all of our peers. Third, we're being really smart with targeted promotions and programs for Florida residents or our Annual Passholder base. We're even doing that with Disney+ members. And maybe finally, we've become -- I talked about this on the last call as well, we've become increasingly sophisticated in how we manage yield and segment our guests.

Per cap growth today, it's more than about just ticket price. And then ultimately, you asked if this is sustainable or how sustainable it is. And I guess the way I'd answer that is we feel very good about the current trends. Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year. And then new capacity and new Experiences they start coming online in 2027. So we keep investing to make the experience fresh and what we see is that drives repeat visits.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. We're going to transition to a technology question on the parks. This is from Rich Greenfield from LightShed Partners. Josh, I'll give this one to you. Where does AI show up in the parks, Rich asks? In the Disney App that could mean an AI concierge that plans a family's Day and rebooks Lightning Lane in real time. Could it also mean ride experiences that become far more personalized? We'd love your big picture thoughts on this topic.

Josh D’Amaro:Great. Okay. Well, thanks, Rich. Well, I think I'll start with the fact that we see AI as a real tailwind for Experiences. And guests already use AI tools to discover what we have to plan. Some are even using it to book their trips now. And ultimately, we want Disney to show up in those tools. And so right now, the team is exploring ways to actually let guests book directly from them. And then on our own channels, we're using AI to make planning and booking easier. These parks, as you know, are big and sometimes they can be complicated. There's a lot to navigate on that front.

There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself. I got to say it's pretty good. And I think it will be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side like a personal concierge that plans and responds the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World. So it's pretty cool, and you can kind of get an indication through that of where we're headed. Rich, you also talked about ride experience.

This isn't necessarily 100% AI, but it is definitely from a technology perspective, you can see how we're bringing things together. Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run. We connected that to Fortnite. We did that back in August. And what guests did on the ride, when they actually rode Millennium Falcon, it unlocked a reward in the game, so that when they went back to the game, that experience carried over into Fortnite. It's pretty cool. And this is just one example that shows how digital and physical experiences can actually reinforce one another in pretty meaningful ways. And so we see a lot more of this ahead. We're also -- we're using AI and advanced analytics for planning in our operations.

And this has given our teams insights to help ensure that we're managing as precisely as we can essentially making sure that the right cast members are in the right place at the right times. And so these technologies are really powerful for us. Maybe just for a moment, let me talk about how we're actually building attractions and what AI is doing on that front because it's pretty amazing. There is no other company that has more than 75 years of like really detailed knowledge about how we build these incredible attractions and experiences. And now we're able to harness all of that information with AI and put it to work in a way that literally nobody else can.

It completely sets us apart, and we're already using this right now to turbocharge how we think about more experiences and more ambitious experiences. Now through all of this, our approach is going to be the same. We will apply technology in a very thoughtful way, our cast members, all of our creative teams, the people that are behind the magic, they'll always stay at the center of the experience.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Our next question is from John Hodulik at UBS. John asks, what are the main areas of focus for the company's new CTO? Can AI drive a meaningful improvement in the customer experience on Disney+ and drive improved efficiency? And can you give examples of both?

Josh D’Amaro:Okay. Great. Thanks, John. Well, first, I just -- I've got to say that we're thrilled to have Karan on the team. He joined us last month. This is our first Chief Technology Officer. He's reporting directly to me. And as I said in my opening remarks, he works across all of our segments and what he's doing is he's modernizing how we build and deliver technology. His remit is across enterprise technology. He has got infrastructure, data and AI platforms. He has got product and engineering. So he's got, again, a really expansive remit. On Disney+, we already use AI to power recommendations and discovery.

And our streaming team, they've made a lot of progress here, and they're giving me regular updates on this. And as that progress is coming to fruition, we're seeing it then in our engagement. And the team is going to keep pressing and I'm going to keep pressing on them, making the products smarter and ultimately better for our subscribers. And then, of course, AI gets even more powerful as we think about our data and unifying our data and our app experience. On the advertising front, we're also leaning pretty heavily into AI. We just actually introduced a couple of new AI advertising products. There's a Creative Studio that turns small businesses' existing brand materials into CTV-ready ads.

So it's pretty powerful. And then there's an agentic ad sales tool that builds advertising campaign proposals. And that latter innovation that I just talked about, it's actually scaled pretty quickly since it launched in August. And the ad team tells me that almost half of all new ad campaigns are actually flowing through that agent, so it's pretty impressive. And then to your question on efficiency. AI helps us work faster across the company, including how we bring content to market. And as I talked about, how we run experiences. On the content side, we're seeing real progress here. AI is accelerating our pre- and post-production processes. Just a small example here.

I don't mean to get overly technical, but we have a new machine learning technology that essentially it sharpens the picture of the films that we're making. And this technology is coming from our own Disney Research Studios and ILM. And what this does basically is it allows us to reduce rendering compute needs by 30% and then delivers cost avoidance and these types of tools are being built by us. And then maybe finally on the Experiences side, I said this just a moment ago. We're using AI in design planning and also using it to help plan our operations a lot more precisely.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. Continuing on the technology front and maybe moving into efficiency for you, Hugh. This is from Sean Diffley at Morgan Stanley. Last quarter, you spoke to being midstream on cost workflows. What is the latest update there? And how should we think about the OpEx savings opportunities across the business and buckets? How big of a role is AI playing in accelerating, and how much of those savings should we expect to be reinvested in the business versus flowing to the bottom line?

Hugh Johnston:Okay. Thanks for the question, Sean. As we discussed last quarter, we are laser-focused on productivity and efficiency, and we've made a lot of progress in that regard. But as a reminder, this exercise is all about enabling greater investment in the long-term growth of the company while simultaneously delivering financial priorities that we've communicated to the market. We are all about delivering the short term and investing in the long term, not an either/or. As we laid out in the letter, we do expect the program to yield roughly $3 billion in run rate savings by fiscal '29.

The efficiencies are going to come from a wide variety of places across the organization and across the functions that we have certainly from procurement and sourcing. In addition to that, IT and real estate consolidation are an opportunity, we'll certainly use shared services as an opportunity as well. And then SG&A efficiencies at each of the segments and at corporate. Again, the important point here is we plan to reinvest the majority of the savings back into the business to drive revenue growth, primarily in streaming and the broader DTC efforts. Those investments will largely take place in content, technology and marketing.

As an example, and as you likely saw in the letter, we're looking at increasing content in fiscal '27 by 9%, particularly in international content. Over the bigger picture as we look at where the savings go, we do expect a portion of the savings to drop to the bottom line. And of course, we'll adjust our plans as business conditions evolve and as we learn as we go through this effort.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. We're going to move to some questions on the Entertainment and DTC front. First question from Michael Ng from Goldman Sachs. And this is for you, Josh. What will the new SVOD vision to be unveiled in spring 2027 include? How will UGC, for example, our TikTok deal, merchandise experiences, generative AI and free tiers play a role?

Josh D’Amaro:Okay. All right. Thanks, Michael. I'm not surprised. This one came up. So let me start with some context first of all. And just from a streaming standpoint, our strategy is built on a couple of different levels. First, we want to make sure that we continue pushing to make our core streaming experience the best it can be, quite frankly, the best in the marketplace. Second, what we want to do is connect our services into a connected ecosystem, and we want to build it on one consumer data set. And that lets us manage toward maximizing fan lifetime value. So let me then start where we are right now.

As this group knows, we had a -- Disney+ had a strong quarter with SVOD revenue growing double digits. And we had healthy engagement growth as well. And we're pretty encouraged by the trends as we head into the fiscal year 2027. And in many ways, right now, you can already see Disney+ becoming that digital home for Disney fans. Disney+ and Hulu, they're coming together in one app. And starting this December, our subscribers will get a fully unified experience. We're adding more live sports from ESPN, along with more podcasts and new content.

And then thinking forward to next month, we'll start introducing creator content through the TikTok agreement that we talked about in the last earnings call, and we're doing more of that as we build towards Avengers: Doomsday. And then just to be clear, we're not launching a new app. We're going to build on the momentum that we have, and you'll start to see more of those elements come to life starting in the spring. And then Michael, you asked about how some other pieces fit in. And here, our ambition is to connect Disney+ more closely with the whole company, with the rest of the company. That means our parks, our cruise ships, merchandise and games.

We know that those are places where fans are already spending a lot of their time and a lot of their money, and we think a stronger connection makes each side just more valuable. And then on AI, as we talked about, we're using it today for recommendations and discovery. And quite frankly, there's a lot more opportunity there over time, and it's something that we'll continue to be thoughtful about. And then you asked about a free tier. We talked about this last quarter that we are exploring a free product. And I think it will reach a more price-sensitive consumer and bring in new Disney+ subscribers. It's going to give us more ad inventory to sell.

It will offer a key retention tool that, quite frankly, we currently don't have. And so ultimately, more connected consumers is clearly better for us. And as this develops, we'll continue to share more with you.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. Another popular question we've been getting. This is from Steven Cahall from Wells Fargo. The licensing deal with Netflix seems bigger and more strategic than those of the recent past and Ted Sarandos even plugged Ice Age on their earnings call. I don't know if you heard about that, Josh.

But that said, we do consider sublicensing really on a case-by-case basis. We don't see it becoming a prominent part of the business by any stretch of the imagination. I also want to close by mentioning that we are super excited about the year ahead for Sports and for ESPN, including our guidance for double-digit segment operating income growth ex the 53rd week, as we laid out in the letter this morning.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. We've got some questions from this morning's shareholder letter. Maybe for you here. This is from Mike Morris, another from Mike Morris at Guggenheim. Can you expand on the decision to change your disclosure at the Entertainment segment? What are the additional revenue details you will share? Also, investors have closely tracked the profit progress at the SVOD business. What is the benefit to the business of removing that disclosure?

Hugh Johnston:Mike, thanks for the question. I'm actually glad you asked this question because I want us to be very clear about this one. As a part of what we've changed, we've actually added additional revenue streams to the disclosure. So you should be able to see those now on our IR website. What you will see is we report SVOD revenues as we have historically, followed by content and IP revenues, which capture content licensing, consumer products licensing, including games and theatrical revenues. And then finally, we've combined the linear networks with the virtual MVPD business.

The benefit here is it gives the investor additional information and a better lens into our content monetization, particularly as we scale SVOD, which is already the largest source of revenue in Entertainment. In terms of removing the SVOD OI disclosure, let me try to summarize our thought process with 3 basic points. First, we're focused on growing SVOD revenues and maximizing the return on our content investment across the entire Entertainment segment, not just one platform's margin within the segment. That's how we manage the business.

Number two, the change gives the team greater flexibility to manage the cost base of the entire portfolio and invest appropriately in our growth business, SVOD, with the goal being faster revenue growth and ultimately, higher term -- higher long-term Entertainment segment operating income. And then last, finally, as we said in the letter and you see in our results, we continue to deliver strong SVOD revenue growth. As we look ahead, we see a long runway for growth at the Entertainment segment through segment margin expansion, with SVOD revenue growth, the key driver of growth and margin at the segment level.

So again, overall, to wrap up, this change really better aligns our disclosure with our strategy of faster revenue growth and maximizing long-term earnings growth, and it matches the way we manage the business internally.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. A question along the same lines for you, Hugh, from Kannan Venkateshwar at Barclays. Streaming profitability improved significantly in the fourth quarter, but you are increasing content and marketing investment in fiscal '27. Should investors expect streaming margins to expand? Or is the priority to reinvest the recent margin upside to accelerate subscriber and revenue growth? Could revenue growth accelerate given the international focus despite the ad headwinds? And then he's got a follow-up. But why do not you maybe take that one first, we'll do the follow-up.

Hugh Johnston:Okay. Good question, Kannan. Our strategy, as we've talked about numerous times in the past is to invest smartly in SVOD to drive SVOD revenue growth. As we said in the letter, we remain focused on SVOD margin expansion over time. And more importantly, we expect Entertainment segment margin to expand as well. SVOD is the biggest business in Entertainment, and that is what drives the segment results. We certainly feel good about the SVOD revenue trends we reported this past quarter and heading into fiscal '27. International content spend will take some time to scale, but we wouldn't make the investment unless we thought it would drive attractive returns.

We continue to exhibit high levels of financial discipline in this business.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Thanks. And his follow-up is, you've announced approximately $3 billion of annual run rate efficiencies by fiscal '29, but much of the savings will be reinvested. What measurable revenue or engagement outcomes should investors use to assess whether that reinvestment is earning an adequate return?

Hugh Johnston:Yes. As you noted, on the $3 billion, we said most of that money will be reinvested, but a portion of it will be dropped to the bottom line as well. This is basically about creating the financial capacity to invest in growth, while also driving more efficiency and speed at our company. You should look to our growth businesses, SVOD and Experiences, along with overall segment operating margin, earnings and FCF to assess our performance and our returns.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:All right. We'll take our last couple of questions from Peter Supino from Wolfe. Back to Experiences, Hugh. Despite the weakness in Asia parks, and only having a partial year benefit from new cruises, you're guiding to high single digit Experiences OI growth, excluding the extra week. What are you seeing across the business that gives you confidence in guiding that level of growth this early in the year?

Hugh Johnston:Yes. Peter, it's really a couple of things. First, kind of zooming out to the most strategic level. Consumers want Experiences now more than ever. We can certainly see that in the feedback that we get from them. So at that high level, there is a strong desire for that. To get a little bit more tactical, certainly as we look at the forward bookings that we see, combined with the capacity that we've added and the demand that we expect in terms of filling that capacity, it gives us high confidence that we'll be able to grow attendance, certainly grow per caps and with that will come the high single digit OI growth.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Great. Thank you. Okay. And then last, Peter asked about our guidance for cash content spend. So on your guidance for 9% cash content spend growth, can you help us think through how much is driven by sports versus -- and films versus programming design for streaming? And of the growth for streaming, what's the strategy in the U.S.?

Hugh Johnston:Yes. It's really investment in all of those areas. We noted that we're growing content spend 9% up to $26 billion. So that's a couple of billion dollar increase. It certainly plays into Sports with the College Football Playoff. In addition to that, international content is a significant growth driver for us as we're seeking to continue to add subscribers in that area. And then, of course, we're looking to make global content through theatrical that will have an impact across the streaming service. So it's not any one thing. It's really all of those things that's driving the growth in spend.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. All right. Thank you, everybody, for joining us this morning. With that, I'm going to hand it back to Josh to wrap up.

Josh D’Amaro:Okay. Thanks, Ben, and thank you all for your time this morning. As you can tell from my remarks today, I am so excited about our future. We've got great stories, passionate fans and we have a team that's executing with real focus. We're building momentum across Experiences and streaming and Sports, and we are excited about what's ahead for 2027. We look forward to continuing to engage with the investment community and our shareholders, including on our Q1 earnings call in February. Thanks for joining, everyone. Have a great Thanksgiving.

With that, let me turn the call back to Ben for analyst Q&A.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Thanks, Josh. Before we turn to Q&A, I want to mention that as highlighted in our shareholder letter and beginning with the first fiscal quarter of 2027, we'll update our disclosure to reflect the shift of consumer products, excluding branded retail, from Disney Experiences to Disney Entertainment, to provide additional revenue disclosure at Disney Entertainment and to exclude equity income from our Entertainment segment operating results. We are providing supplemental financial information reflecting these changes available on our Investor Relations website.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:All right. We're going to begin our Q&A with questions on our Experiences segment. First question comes from Ric Prentiss of Raymond James. Ric asks, several big additions coming to the Orlando and other parks in the near to midterm, which ones are the most significant in terms of new capacity? And do you see those as growth accelerators or primarily to maintain current growth levels? Any thoughts or insights on the return of capital targets? Josh, do you want to take that one?

Josh D’Amaro:Yes, I'll take that. Thanks for the question, Ric. Maybe before I answer the question, I understand from my team that you are retiring soon, and that you've done something like 120 earnings calls. I don't know what to say about that, but congratulations to you. We obviously wish you all the best. Back to your question. So before I answer it directly, maybe I'll just take a beat here and reflect on the year that we just had. It was a great one. We had a new record number of guests come to our attractions all around the world. And yes, you're right, there's a lot going on right now.

We have more projects underway all around the world at any other point in the history of the segment. And a lot of that is actually focused right at -- in Orlando at Walt Disney World. I was just there recently, and I get a chance to go every once in a while and walk the projects under construction. And I got to say the Imagineers are just -- they're doing an incredible job over delivering on creative expectations that I have and the scale and the detail across all the expansion that's taking place there. It's really incredible. The last stop on my trip was at Monstropolis, which is at the studio. And it's again, the scale is fantastic.

It's just stunning. I think once we get a chance to open this up to guests, they're going to love it. We shared this in the past, these additions, all this expansion, it comes online over a period of time. The first phase of it with things like Monstropolis that I just mentioned, Lakeshore Lodge and Tropical Americas, which is Animal Kingdom, they all open in calendar 2027. And we haven't announced the dates on some of the other things like new Cars -- the new Cars Land and Villains Land at Magic Kingdom but they will follow after that.

If we go to the West Coast in Anaheim, Avengers Campus, which is at Disney California Adventure, that's going to double in size by 2028. So a pretty significant expansion there. And as this group knows, we're investing across all of our international parks as well. Now each of these are expected to contribute to growth. Some of the projects will add capacity to the parks that they're in. Others will give guests more reason to come and visit, maybe they'll stay longer. Hopefully, they spend a little bit more or do some of all of those things. And of course, that's going to let us grow both volume and yield, which you've seen in our results.

And then on returns, we stay disciplined. Every project is going to go through a rigorous review. Each one has clear return expectations. We're not adding capacity for its own sake, we pair that with strong guest demand. And as I had mentioned last quarter, we're investing to deliver double-digit returns over the lifetime of these projects.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. Next question is from Jessica Reif Ehrlich from BofA. Jessica asks, Experience is in the middle of one of the largest expansions ever. Cruise state room capacity is up roughly 50% with Destiny and Adventure. Fleet is heading towards 13 ships over the next 5 years, and you're adding new attractions at Walt Disney World in 2027. So the question is, how confident are you that demand keeps pace without leaning on promotions? Specifically, what are advanced bookings telling you about yield on the new ships, especially in Asia, where your parks are soft? How do you sustain segment margins through a period of heavy preopening costs and new capacity?

Josh D’Amaro:That's for me.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:That's for you, Josh. Yes, sorry.

Josh D’Amaro:Okay. All right. Well, thanks, Jessica. All right. So you asked about demand keeping pace with the added capacity. First, remember, we are a small -- really small share of the global cruise industry today. And we've got really unique competitive advantages in this market. Our cruise line, it draws on all the great IP that we have and the connection that we have with our fans and our guests. So we think that there's a lot of room to grow on this front. The real limit, I guess, on how fast we grow cruise is it's shipbuilding capacity itself, not necessarily the market opportunity. Hugh and I talk about this a lot.

We would add more ships if we could get ones that meet the standards that we have. And then this business, cruise, it's really flexible. We can add, we can reposition capacity faster than we can build land-based resort and that lets us reach new guests and go to new markets. By the way, just as an example, next summer, the Disney Wish sails in the U.K. and Europe. So we've got a lot of flexibility on that front. On your question about Asia, so we called out consumer pressure at our Shanghai and Hong Kong parks in the letter. And we're expecting that will continue into fiscal '27.

I think it's worth mentioning in the fourth quarter, strength at our domestic parks and at Disneyland Paris, it more than offset that weakness. And this is just a byproduct of our portfolio, which really is built to absorb these kinds of swings in specific market conditions. Now we're entering our second year with the Adventure. So it's too early to tell if the macro weakness is impacting demand for that single ship. But for the rest of the fleet, when we look at booked occupancy, it's actually holding up pretty nicely even with the additional capacity that we brought online. So we feel good about forward cruise bookings. And then margins.

So lastly, on the margin side, we don't break out cruise specifically, but what we have done is grown our margins in our domestic Parks & Experiences by just about 300 basis points over the last 10 years. And we have to, of course, think about preopening costs as a normal part of launching new ships and attractions. So I think I covered most of them.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Yes. Okay. Hugh, this is for you from Laura Martin at Needham. With Disney several years into its $60 billion 10-year capital investment program, can you talk us through the relative ROIC of parks versus cruise ships, and whether we eventually reach a saturation point where there is cannibalization between the 2?

Hugh Johnston:Yes. Great. Thanks for the question, Laura. A lot of questions on cruises and parks this morning. We believe we're uniquely positioned because of the breadth and connectivity of the portfolio that we have. And in a lot of ways, cruise is a great example of that. On the one hand, we have a large funnel of fans that enjoy the land-based offerings and then we can introduce them into the Cruise Lines. At the same time, by virtue of the mobility of the Cruise Lines, it allows us to reach new geographies and new guests that might not otherwise be able to get to our parks.

And that kind of reinforces why we see parks and cruises as complementary growth platforms rather than competing investments. As Josh mentioned earlier, we're really turbocharging the business at a faster pace than we have historically. And the ROIC is a mix of the mature cash-generating investments along with projects that are still work in process or under development. If you look only at the assets that are open and operating, returns remain really strong, and we expect that strength to carry through as the new investments come online as well.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. Thank you, Hugh. I guess as a retirement gift, we've got another question from Ric. I think, Josh, for you. As everyone is aware, there's been a divergence recently in Disney's domestic parks performance versus the competition. What can we attribute that to? And how sustainable is that trend?

Josh D’Amaro:Okay. Again, thanks, Ric. Actually, I'm glad you noticed that. I mean, listen, for more than 70 years now, our parks have been how families spend time together. And that connection that we have with our fans, it's just a huge reason that we stand apart from anyone else. Of course, we bring the best IP in the world and that IP just keeps that flywheel spinning and giving people and fans, new reasons to engage with us. And yes, I mean, the business is good. We saw healthy growth in both volume and per capita spending at Walt Disney World this summer. And if you look at domestic parks in the quarter, volume was up.

So attendance was up 3%. That's excluding the 53rd week and per caps were also up, they were up 4%. And when you step back and look at it, there are a few things that are driving this growth. First, I think it's so clear, fans just value the Disney Experiences, and there really isn't anything out there that matches it. And in many ways, Experiences is where our flywheel and our super fans, they come together most clearly, and you see it in our financial results. Second, consumers want real Experiences now. And I think that we're seeing that accelerate. People today are spending so much of their lives on screens.

They're just looking for time to connect with each other in the real world. And I think Disney is -- a Disney park, it's one of the few places that you can actually do that. We deliver on that at scale, and that puts us in a very different position from almost all of our peers. Third, we're being really smart with targeted promotions and programs for Florida residents or our Annual Passholder base. We're even doing that with Disney+ members. And maybe finally, we've become -- I talked about this on the last call as well, we've become increasingly sophisticated in how we manage yield and segment our guests.

Per cap growth today, it's more than about just ticket price. And then ultimately, you asked if this is sustainable or how sustainable it is. And I guess the way I'd answer that is we feel very good about the current trends. Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year. And then new capacity and new Experiences they start coming online in 2027. So we keep investing to make the experience fresh and what we see is that drives repeat visits.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Okay. We're going to transition to a technology question on the parks. This is from Rich Greenfield from LightShed Partners. Josh, I'll give this one to you. Where does AI show up in the parks, Rich asks? In the Disney App that could mean an AI concierge that plans a family's Day and rebooks Lightning Lane in real time. Could it also mean ride experiences that become far more personalized? We'd love your big picture thoughts on this topic.

Josh D’Amaro:Great. Okay. Well, thanks, Rich. Well, I think I'll start with the fact that we see AI as a real tailwind for Experiences. And guests already use AI tools to discover what we have to plan. Some are even using it to book their trips now. And ultimately, we want Disney to show up in those tools. And so right now, the team is exploring ways to actually let guests book directly from them. And then on our own channels, we're using AI to make planning and booking easier. These parks, as you know, are big and sometimes they can be complicated. There's a lot to navigate on that front.

There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself. I got to say it's pretty good. And I think it will be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side like a personal concierge that plans and responds the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World. So it's pretty cool, and you can kind of get an indication through that of where we're headed. Rich, you also talked about ride experience.

This isn't necessarily 100% AI, but it is definitely from a technology perspective, you can see how we're bringing things together. Millennium Falcon: Smugglers Run. We connected that to Fortnite. We did that back in August. And what guests did on the ride, when they actually rode Millennium Falcon, it unlocked a reward in the game, so that when they went back to the game, that experience carried over into Fortnite. It's pretty cool. And this is just one example that shows how digital and physical experiences can actually reinforce one another in pretty meaningful ways. And so we see a lot more of this ahead. We're also -- we're using AI and advanced analytics for planning in our operations.

And this has given our teams insights to help ensure that we're managing as precisely as we can essentially making sure that the right cast members are in the right place at the right times. And so these technologies are really powerful for us. Maybe just for a moment, let me talk about how we're actually building attractions and what AI is doing on that front because it's pretty amazing. There is no other company that has more than 75 years of like really detailed knowledge about how we build these incredible attractions and experiences. And now we're able to harness all of that information with AI and put it to work in a way that literally nobody else can.

It completely sets us apart, and we're already using this right now to turbocharge how we think about more experiences and more ambitious experiences. Now through all of this, our approach is going to be the same. We will apply technology in a very thoughtful way, our cast members, all of our creative teams, the people that are behind the magic, they'll always stay at the center of the experience.

Benjamin Daniel Swinburne, C.F.A.:Our next question is from John Hodulik at UBS. John asks, what are the main areas of focus for the company's new CTO? Can AI drive a meaningful improvement in the customer experience on Disney+ and drive improved efficiency? And can you give examples of both?
